hypothesis: If Darwin's inference holds, the numerically dated end of the Secondary (Mesozoic) period, and specifically the top of the Chalk (Cretaceous), lies more than about 300 million years before present on the International Chronostratigraphic Chart.
pass_criterion: The ICS chart gives the top of the Cretaceous (the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary, which marks the end of the Chalk-depositing Secondary) an age of at least 300 Ma. Darwin's 'far more than 300 million years' would then be consistent with the data.
fail_criterion: The ICS chart gives the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary an age below 300 Ma. I expect about 66 Ma, and the base of the Upper Cretaceous at about 100 Ma is also below 300 Ma. Either value refutes the claim that more than 300 million years have elapsed since the latter part of the Secondary period.
interpretation: Darwin's 'latter part of the Secondary period' is read as the Late Cretaceous, when the Chalk was deposited, and its upper limit is the K–Pg boundary. 'Years elapsed' is read as the numerical age in Ma of that boundary. His erosion-rate arithmetic (1 inch per century on a 500-foot cliff) is not tested directly. The test checks only the quantity he infers, the elapsed time. Modern reinterpretation: the Weald denudation began after Cretaceous deposition and Cenozoic uplift, so it took far less than the whole time since the Chalk, which makes the test conservative against Darwin. The Secondary corresponds roughly to the Mesozoic (252–66 Ma).

dataset.name: International Chronostratigraphic Chart
dataset.why_it_fits: The chart is the standard reference for numeric boundary ages of geological periods and stages. The fields used are the unit names (Cretaceous, Upper Cretaceous stages, Paleogene) and the numeric ages in Ma of their boundaries, in particular the base of the Paleogene (K–Pg boundary, about 66 Ma). The chart can be downloaded as PDF, image and machine-readable files from the landing page.
